prompt: Write a personal essay about moving to a new city. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
The first week in a new city is mostly about finding things. You look for the grocery store that doesn't charge four dollars for a lime, the laundromat that stays open past nine, the route to work that doesn't require a transfer. I spent my first several days in the new apartment walking with my phone held out in front of me like a compass, and I got lost anyway, because a map shows you where things are but not how to belong near them.

I had chosen the move myself, which made it harder to complain about. The old city had gotten small in the way a coat gets small: nothing wrong with it, but I kept catching myself in the same rooms, having the same conversations with the same people about the same traffic. I wanted to be a stranger for a while. I wanted the particular humility of not knowing which bus to take.

The apartment was on the third floor of a brick building with radiators that knocked all night like someone wanting in. The windows faced a bakery, and every morning around five the smell of bread found its way up through the open gap I never could fully close. I liked that about the place before I liked anything else. It felt like the city was making an offer I hadn't earned yet.

What nobody tells you about moving is how much of your identity is held up by small, repeated interactions. In the old city, the barista knew my order. The man at the hardware store asked about my dog. The neighbor and I nodded at each other in the stairwell for six years and that nod meant something. In the new city, I was a face without a history. I ordered coffee and said "thanks" and got back a polite nothing. For the first month, I felt almost transparent, like I could walk through a room and leave no mark.

I did what people do. I said yes to things I would have skipped. I went to a trivia night at a bar where I knew no one and answered two questions correctly and felt absurdly proud. I joined a running group that met at six on Saturdays, and I was slower than everyone, and they waited for me at every corner anyway without making a show of it. I learned that loneliness in a new place is not a feeling so much as a shape: you notice the empty chairs at a table, the phone that doesn't ring, the weekend that stretches out with nothing in it.

The turn came in an ordinary way. I was buying bread from the bakery below my window, a loaf I'd started buying because I couldn't stop smelling it. The woman at the counter, who had flour on her forearms and a pencil behind one ear, asked if I was the new person upstairs. I said yes. She said she'd noticed I came in on Tuesdays and Fridays. I hadn't realized I had a pattern. It was a small thing, but it was the first time someone in this city had seen me as a fact rather than a visitor. I walked home holding the warm bag against my chest like it was something I'd been given.

That's the thing I think about now when people ask whether moving was worth it. The city didn't welcome me in any dramatic sense. It just kept being there, repeatedly, until I started to be there too. Belonging turned out to be an accumulation of tiny recognitions: the bakery woman, the runners who waited, the bus driver who said good morning to everyone and then, one day, to me by name because I'd told him once. None of it was big. All of it added up.

I still miss the old city, sometimes sharply, usually at unexpected moments, like when I hear a song that was playing in a car we drove everywhere in. Grief for a place is real even when you chose to leave it. But I've also noticed that I have started to know things here that I couldn't have known anywhere else. I know which corner floods when it rains. I know the bakery closes early on Mondays. I know that the radiators knock because the building is old and breathing, and that the sound, which annoyed me in October, now feels like the building saying it's still here.

Moving teaches you that a home is not a place you arrive at but a set of habits you slowly build, one Tuesday at a time. You stand in a line you don't yet understand, you get a loaf of bread, and someone notices you came back. That noticing is most of what I was looking for, though I didn't know it when I left.
